full_judgment: 8. I have perused the revisional application along with the judgments of the Courts below and the materials on record and heard the learned lawyers appearing on behalf of the petitioner and the opposite parties. It appears that the trial Court found the agreement in question to be a forged one. The defendant pleaded a case of fraud and forgery which was not proved by evidence. In cases of fraud, collusion or undue influence the onus is on the party who alleges it as such to prove the allegation. There is a presumption of good faith on human transaction as there is a presumption of innocence in criminal matter and, that being so, the burden of proving every species of bad faith such as fraud, collusion, forgery, etc, rushes on the person who asserts the same. The lower appellate Court believed the document to be genuine and has observed, that the trial Court has misconceived and misconstrued the facts of the suit. It further appears that the plaintiff filed the original copy of the agreement before the trial Court on 11-4-81 with the attached list and on 27-2-83 he filed an application before the trial Court for getting back the original copy of the agreement and the said application was allowed by the order dated 27-2-83 and he took back the original copy of the same. On 22-9-84 he filed the said original copy of the agreement again with a firstly but due to inadvertence there is no record of it in the order sheet and when the deed was found to be missing he brought it to the notice of the Court by an application dated 30-12-84 but there was no order on that application. The trial Court allowed the use of the photocopy of the original agreement on evidence. It appears that the trial Court was fully satisfied about the whereabouts of the original copy of the agreement and its execution and it was marked as Exhibit-I by the trial Court as per the order of the appellate Court correcting its own omission. The appellate Court found that all the documents are in the record but the exhibit list has not been prepared, signed, sealed and exhibits were not marked and by the order dated 19-10-94 the lower appellate Court sent the record to the trial Court to have the exhibit list prepared, signed, sealed and marked and the trial Court corrected the omission. Rules or procedures are made to subserve the ends of justice and not to defeat them. Mere omission to sign and seal exhibits or deposition sheets does not affect the merit of the case nor the jurisdiction of the Court and such omissions are mere defects or irregularities in the procedure and not an illegality when section 99 of the Code of Civil Procedure aims to prevent such procedural technicalities. Non compliance of the procedure for marking the exhibits and to prepare the exhibits list does not destroy the validity of the Court proceeding. It appears that the plaintiff has discharged the primary onus to prove the genuineness of the disputed agreement. The Court may at any stage of the suit reject any document which it considers irrelevant or inadmissible after recording the grounds. No plea was taken in the Courts below about the admissibility of the document which was proved by PW s 1, 2 and 3. The trial Court failed to appreciate how to prove a document as per section 73 of the Evidence Act and what constitutes forgery of a document under sections 463 and 464 of the Penal Code. The defendant No. 1 in his written statement only alleged that the document is forged and created but did not prove such allegation by adducing evidence during trial. Though the defendant pleaded a case of fraud and forgery he did not lead any evidence to preve the same and mere statement in the written statement is not enough nor it is an evidence by itself unless such statement is proved by leading evidence by its maker. It is now a settled principle of law that unless objection as to admissibility of a document was taken at the earlier opportunity i.e. at the time of admitting the document into evidence, the question of its admissibility cannot be raised at a subsequent stage. Although the date of execution of both the safkabala deed and the agreement of reconveyance was on 19-7-69 but the stamp of agreement was purchased earlier and there is no illegality in purchasing the stamp. On the permission of the trial Court the photocopy was used during taking of evidence before the trial Court and after being fully satisfied it was treated as exhibit-1 by the trial Court. The lower appellate Court disbelieved the case of the defendant No.3.
